In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and I invoke blessings and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and whoever is guided by his guidance and follows his practice until the Day of Judgement. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God Most High and His blessings.

To proceed: God, Glorified and Exalted, built this worldly life upon fixed norms that do not change. These norms are from the command of God, Glorified and Exalted, and from His decree, and they cannot fail to hold, just as the turning of the celestial sphere and the succession of night and day do not fail. Among these norms is the linkage of causes to their effects. Calling people to Islam (daʿwah) is a cause of guidance, but it does not lead to this result unless it proceeds according to its own norm and according to what God intended for it. The guidance to which the call leads is the guidance of direction — that is, illuminating the path for people, so that they know what they were created for, what their Lord, Glorified and Exalted, has commanded them, and what the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) brought them..

It is not possible to illuminate this path for people unless this call is governed by the controls of the Sharia and connected to the prophetic method that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) followed, which is the successful method and the model for treading the path of truth. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) made that clear when he said: "I have left you upon a white highway" — or "upon something like the white one" — "its night like its day; none deviates from it but one who perishes."

What the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) left us upon is what God has approved for the two weighty kinds, humankind and the jinn. It is God's straight method, and it is His path leading to His Garden, and it is His firm rope: whoever holds fast to it is protected. This firm rope upon which the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) left us is like the white highway, its night like its day; and this requires the clarification of every confusion and error that occurs in it, and guarantees that error can be known from correctness when there is confusion. For if the matter were entrusted to men's independent reasoning it would change and be altered, as was the case with the earlier religions, whose preservation was entrusted to their own adherents — and you see what happened to them of distortion and alteration.

As for this religion sent down upon Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), it is protected from change and alteration: falsehood does not come to it from before it or from behind it, a sending down from One Wise, Praiseworthy. God has undertaken its preservation and has taken charge of that Himself; He did not entrust it to an angel brought near nor to a prophet sent. So it is preserved by the preservation of God, Glorified and Exalted, the Living, the Sustainer, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes; He does not sleep and it does not befit Him to sleep; the affairs of the night are raised to Him before the day and the affairs of the day before the night. Therefore no disorder and no discrepancy can occur in it without its error becoming clear to people and its falsity becoming plain to them; and that is part of God's protection of His straight path.

Among the wisdoms of this is that after the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) no messenger will come to humanity; no prophet can come after him, for he is the seal of the prophets. If the matter were entrusted permanently to men's independent reasoning and to their correction, that would entail its passing away and people's needing someone to renew it. But God, Glorified and Exalted, undertook its preservation, and He knew that He would send no messenger after Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him).

Therefore whoever treads the path of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) must tread it with clear insight into it, and must come to know the controls of his travelling, the bends of his road and the problems that arise for him on this road. Hence it is incumbent upon us, in the discourse of the call presented to people — in which the one who gives it stands in place of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), and discharges in it the trust of God which He offered to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, and they refused to bear it and were afraid of it, and the human being bore it; and which the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) entrusted to us to convey to people in the last address he made to people, when he said: "Let the one present among you convey to the one absent, for many a one to whom it is conveyed retains it better than one who hears it."

He entrusted us with preserving it too, and mentioned the great merit of whoever preserves it, saying, in what the compilers of the Sunan books recorded from him in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him): "May God brighten a man who hears my words, retains them, and conveys them as he heard them; for many a bearer of understanding is not himself a person of understanding, and many a bearer of understanding bears it to one who understands better than he does." And he made clear too the office of those who guard it and expound it to people, in what Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr recorded in the introduction to al-Tamhīd and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi in Sharaf Aṣḥāb al-Ḥadīth, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him), that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "This knowledge will be carried by the upright of every generation, who will ward off from it the distortion of the extremists, the false claims of the falsifiers, and the misinterpretation of the ignorant."

So this clear insight into the matter to which a person calls is one of the most important controls of the discourse of the call. One who wants to call without knowledge, and does not want to be connected to the practice of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) or to his method, and does not want to tread the path of those who preceded him, nor to benefit from what they were upon and what they took up — such a one must fall into the mire. There must therefore be this clear insight, which requires that a person know his proof in everything he takes up, and that he have a warrant from God, Glorified and Exalted, in everything he does. Whoever is upon that is upon a light from his Lord: if he halts, he halts on the basis of knowledge, and if he advances, he advances on the basis of knowledge; and whoever is like this does not doubt in any matter and nothing of the doubtful things is obscure to him.

Then after this, likewise, there must be another control, more emphatic than the one before it, namely sincerity (ikhlāṣ) towards God, Glorified and Exalted, and intending His noble face in the whole matter. Every discourse a person offers on the path of the call, he must be sincere in it towards God Most High, or else its harm will be greater than its benefit. A person must be sincere in every word that issues from him and every act that issues from him; otherwise the absence of sincerity harms both the giver of the discourse and its hearer severely. Therefore sincerity must be reviewed in every statement a person makes, and he must know that the word he says is a trust in his keeping, and that it will be put before him in the presence of God, in the record fastened to his neck; and his own limbs will bear witness against him as to what he said, and the noble angels, declared pure with God Most High, will bear witness against him as to what he uttered.

Then after this there must be another control, the control of moderation and balance in the matter; for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) warned against extravagance and warned likewise against excess and against negligence. This discourse must therefore be a middle course between excess and negligence. Excess requires of a person that he overdo the matter in a way that takes him outside the scope of the Sharia, and at that point personal desire (hawā) must enter into it; and personal desire is the opposite of the Sharia, and one who holds fast to it is worshipping a partner set up with God, namely desire. Desire is one of the partners worshipped besides God, Mighty and Majestic; and one who clings to his desire and gives it precedence over God's address is censured in the Qur'an with the utmost censure, for he has taken his desire as his god. You know that it is made clear in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt that this is a cause of entering the Fire, and that opposing desire and restraining the soul from desire is a cause of entering the Garden.

Then after this a person must grasp the meaning of this moderation, and that the excess that is forbidden is not the exceeding of what people were upon, nor the exceeding of the stage a person himself was in. Rather, what is meant by the prohibition of excess is exceeding the prophetic method. So if we are in one of the stages of our weakness, or in the stage of seeking and increasing in knowledge, or in a stage of being under-resourced in means, and we take up what we have and what we are able to do, and then a fresh blessing comes from God, Glorified and Exalted, which permits an increase in performance and in giving — then putting that blessing to work is not excess, nor extremism, nor overstepping.

Similarly, on the other side, He forbade negligence, which is falling short, and reclining into ease, and clinging to the earth. This negligence requires of a person that he leave some of what the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) brought, and send it back to God, Glorified and Exalted, so that he becomes selective: whatever agrees with his desire and suits his time he takes up, and whatever opposes it he leaves. You know that whoever does that is not sincere towards God, Glorified and Exalted; rather he takes what he wants and rejects what he wants. God has made clear that this is the way of the hypocrites: {And when they are called to God and His Messenger so that he may judge between them, at once a party of them turns away. But if the right is theirs, they come to him submissively. Is there sickness in their hearts, or have they doubted, or do they fear that God and His Messenger will deal unjustly with them? Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers} (Sūrat al-Nūr 24:48–50).

There must therefore be surrender to the whole of God's command; otherwise what is the difference between the Muslims and the Jews, if the Muslim takes what agrees with him and leaves what opposes him? Is that not what the Jews say? They say: we believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part. Did they not say to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and to the believers with him: we will obey you at the start of the day and oppose you for the rest of it? So the Muslim must surrender to the whole of God's command and take up the whole of the method; and God has made that a condition of faith, for He said: "But no, by your Lord, they do not believe until they make you judge in what has arisen between them, and then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit in full submission."

Likewise this middle method is useful in this discourse of the call in other respects. Among them is that it brings a person to what he cannot reach by himself, with his own energies and his limited means. For when a person takes up this balanced, middle method, in which there is neither excess nor negligence, events do not provoke him: when inducement and intimidation come, they have no effect upon him; when ease and blessing come, they do not make him overstep; and when adversity and trial come, they likewise do not abase him, and do not turn him back from what he has taken up.

Then after this, this control must be taken up in what concerns dealing with people. For people's hearts rarely come together upon a matter, and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said of them: "People are like a hundred camels: you can scarcely find among them one fit to ride." So if a person inclines with some of them at the expense of others, that will lead the others to aversion. It is soundly established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) passed by some people of the Ansar competing in archery — that is, shooting at a target they had set up — and said: "Shoot, and I am with the clan of so-and-so." So the others held back. He said: "What is the matter with you?" They said: "How can we compete against them when you are with them?" He said: "Shoot, and I am with all of you."

So this balance is necessary, and it entails the gathering of hearts; while its opposite, in turn, entails division, disagreement and strife. For if a person departs from this middle course and inclines to the side of excess and exaggeration, his discourse of the call is often an arousal that reaches the point of explosion without that being put to use in its proper orbit and on its straight course. And likewise, if it comes with coldness and lifelessness and does not achieve the purpose intended by this discourse, that too is a cause of people slipping away from around him and not taking up what he says.

Then after this, that often leads also to unpraiseworthy reactions, such as what happens on many occasions of some people declaring others unbelievers (takfīr) on no legal basis. Declaring unbelief is not censured in the Sharia absolutely; rather, the declaring of unbelief that is censured in the Sharia is the declaring of Muslims to be unbelievers — the declaring of unbelief against one who has taken up Islam and is right in it: this is what is censured in the Sharia. As for declaring unbelievers to be unbelievers, that is not censured in the Sharia, and no person of sense could censure it.

Then after this, among the results of this moderation is also that it makes turning back possible, and makes it possible to take up the more balanced line. If the error in some of those particulars and steps becomes clear to a person, he is able to turn back at close range and is not then at a point where he cannot turn back. You know that on the motorways, if a person takes the outermost lane, he cannot turn back if he wants to, nor stop at all, because he has reached the end in that lane. So if a person wants to stop or to turn back, let him take the middle, or the lane that allows him to turn back.

Likewise, among the controls of this discourse is that it be with the people. If the discourse of the call occupies people with what they do not live in their daily lives and do not find in their reality, or is occupied away from what concerns them and in which they spend their working hours, then it is a failed discourse, because it is in one valley and the people are in another. It must therefore be concerned with people's concerns, and must accompany people in their developments and their circumstances. Hence the discourse of the call is bound to its time and its place. For us to speak now, for example, of what people were speaking about at the beginning of the spread of this revival — the fitness of Islam to be applied, or the like of that framing which you find in the old books written at the beginning of the revival — is to take up what is no longer a subject of debate, and to go backwards in the middle, in the course of the road; so it cannot be taken up. Its likeness is that of someone who has reached fifth gear in his speed and then wants to drop straight from it to second gear, for example, or to third, without passing through fourth: this damages his car and does not enable him to reach his goal.

What people live and are concerned with is taken into account in the Sharia. In his sermons and in his directing of people, the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) used to speak about the events people were witnessing, and to speak about what related to their daily life. You know his address to the believers at the expedition of al-Muraysi', when rancour and hatred arose between the water-drawer of the Emigrants and the water-drawer of the Helpers, and this one said, "To me, Emigrants!" and the other said, "To me, Helpers!" and he said: "Is it the call of the Jahiliyyah, while I am among you? Leave it, for it is putrid."

For the people of the Jahiliyyah, when a disagreement occurred between them, each one of them would raise the rallying cry of the Jahiliyyah and call upon his own folk and his supporters, each drawing strength against the other through his tribe. Then the Islamic call came and rejected this pattern entirely. And as for the Emigrants and the Helpers, rallying by them is not a rallying by tribes nor by factions; it is a call by a noble legal title, for God, Glorified and Exalted, honoured the Emigrants among the believers by their emigration to God and His Messenger, and honoured the Helpers by the emigration of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) to them. Yet despite that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) rejects rallying by this cry, because of its resemblance to the rallying of the people of the Jahiliyyah by their cries, and he treats it exactly like the rallying of the people of the Jahiliyyah, saying: "Is it the call of the Jahiliyyah, while I am among you? Leave it, for it is putrid."

Likewise, his concern in his discourse of the call with people's affairs and with what they live combined the affair of this world and the affair of the Hereafter. As for what relates to the affair of the Hereafter, you have heard an example of it; and as for what relates to the affairs of this world, an instance is his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), in what Aisha narrated in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections concerning the sermon for rain, that he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "You have complained of the drought of your lands and of the rain being delayed beyond its proper season; and God has commanded you to call upon Him and has promised you that He will answer you." Then he said: "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Master of the Day of Judgement. There is no god but God; He does what He wills. O God, You are God; there is no god but You. You are the Self-Sufficient and we are the ones in need of You. Send down upon us the rain, and make what You send down a strength for us and a provision for a time."

Here the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) spoke about a matter that concerned people among the affairs of their world, namely the drought, hardship, distress and straitened livelihood they were in. He spoke of that in his sermon and said: "You have complained of the drought of your lands and of the rain being delayed beyond its proper season," and he mentioned the legal remedies, namely that God, Glorified and Exalted, had commanded them to call upon Him and had promised them that He would answer them when they called upon Him.

Further, in his attention to what people live of the affairs of their lives, the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) used to relate to them what resembled those affairs from the lives of others, so that they might be experiences for them — even in domestic and private affairs. Thus Aisha, the Mother of the Believers, narrates from him the hadith of Umm Zar' in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, in which the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) made clear that he was to Aisha as Abu Zar' was to Umm Zar', except that he would not divorce her. This hadith contains mention of many social situations within the particulars of the household, and some of the concerns of women and what they meet with in their houses by way of hardship; and at the beginning of the hadith: "Eleven women sat down and pledged and covenanted with one another that they would conceal nothing of the news of their husbands."

These examples of people's lives, their conduct and their social dealings, and the Prophet's attention to them and his expounding of them to his community — all of that falls within this framework and within the scope of the discourse of the call living with people's concerns and with what they are in. Among the problems are those that recur in every situation, namely the social matters that people live: the concerns of the household and the problems of the relationship between husband and wife; likewise the raising of children; likewise matters of livelihood and what arises in it of straitness and ease; likewise matters of neighbours and their rights. These are recurring matters that must be treated in the discourse of the call, and must take their appropriate space in it, because they are what people live and what recurs in their daily life.

Like that are the affairs of the world around us. Among the controls of the discourse of the call it is necessary that it address these concerns and affairs, for these human beings are all connected in circles of connection, the far and the near alike within them. The world today has become like a single village, and the media and the means of communication assist in that. So whoever does not attend to civilisation and its aspects and their transmission, and to the kinds of patterns of people's living and what relates to that, is bound to be overtaken by something of what he had guarded against in his own country. Today, if we do not talk about the aspects of Westerners' lives and what they live in their countries — what of it is positive and what of it is negative — that will overtake us in our countries, and will come through the media, which we are unable to influence; and many will take on its character: those defeated under the pressure of this life, and those dazzled by Western material life. Hence the discourse of the call must convey the experiences of others, and must be informed about the circulation of this civilisation, its rise and its decline, and about what relates to that of effects upon people's psychology, their culture and their interests.

Likewise, among these controls is that sound discourse of the call must take part in forming the public opinion of these human beings. These human beings act on the basis of conviction, and this conviction is not an innate disposition upon which God created people; rather God Most High said: {And God brought you forth from the bellies of your mothers knowing nothing} (Sūrat al-Naḥl 16:78). But God gave us means of surveying what is around us, through which we come to our convictions — these are what convictions are formed through. Hence He said: {And God brought you forth from the bellies of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing and sight and hearts}. So these are the means of encompassing what is around us, and public opinion is formed through them. Likewise He said in enumerating His favour upon the human being: {Have We not made for him two eyes, and a tongue and two lips, and guided him to the two highways?} (Sūrat al-Balad 90:8–10). So these means with which God has favoured him, people will put to use, and their use of them entails coming to know what is around them, and through that the convictions become entrenched in them upon which they build their positions and their conduct.

Hence the basic influences on public opinion are: first, the home in which a person is brought up; second, the school in which he studies; third, the street in which he lives; fourth, the media he listens to; fifth, the influence of companionship — and the call enters into this — the influence of companionship, that is, of people's ethics and their dealings. These are the five influences through which a person's general outlook, which we call public opinion, is built, and on the basis of which positions are taken. In our own time we have been afflicted with the corruption of most of these means, their deviation, and their not being put to proper use.

So, for example, the discourse of the call must have an effect upon the soundness of homes, because the home is the first means that influences the public opinion of those brought up in it. Second, the discourse of the call must likewise have an effect in the schools in which people study, because these schools influence their convictions and their interests. Notice that students who study in schools and take various subjects from various teachers will, by the end of their graduation from that school, have convictions entrenched in them: one group of them will be influenced by the teacher of one of those subjects and so will take an interest in that subject; another group is not influenced by any of the teachers, but a subject appealed to them and they tasted it, so they took an interest in that subject; and another group saw the whole thing as a burden and a weariness, and was influenced by that into withdrawal and seclusion and into cutting short the course of learning and its path. This is what you witness in every school from which people graduate, and this is among the influences upon public opinion. So the discourse of the call must enter the schools so as to have an effect in the choice of specialisations, in the choice of teachers' methods, in the assessment of persons, and even in the choice to continue on the path of seeking knowledge and in spurring people on to that.

Likewise, the third institution influencing public opinion is the street, and this too the discourse of the call must enter with strength, because of the great danger in it to which the noble Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) alerted us in the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him) in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, when he said: "Beware of sitting in the roads." They said: "Messenger of God, we cannot do without our sitting places, in which we converse." He said: "Then if you insist on the sitting place, give the road its due." They said: "And what is the due of the road, Messenger of God?" He said: "Lowering the gaze, restraining harm, returning the greeting of peace, enjoining right and forbidding wrong." These are the aspects of the discourse of the call entering the street: "lowering the gaze, restraining harm, returning the greeting of peace, enjoining right and forbidding wrong." If these appear in the street, then it will have a positive influence, and the information received by way of it, or the character acquired by way of it, will lead to the required result in soundness.

Then after this, the fourth institution is the media. These means people hear whether they are willing or unwilling. Many a person has the pastime of following the media: he listens to the news bulletin on a particular radio station, and when it ends he moves the dial to another station which will repeat the same words to him, and then he moves to another station, and so on. Likewise others also have this pastime of following television screens: they move from channel to channel, and whenever a programme ends or a channel's transmission ends they move from it to another channel. Others again are occupied with the print media: no column is written in a newspaper or a magazine but they follow it, and most of their time is occupied with that. And others again are occupied with the medium that is the most widespread — or the most stirring — in our time, namely the internet: they follow sites numbered in the hundreds of thousands and are occupied with them, so that it takes up a great space of their time and their interests.

There is no doubt that this pastime must have an effect upon the one who practises it. A person who has heard a news item five times, and has heard its analysis from several angles as well, is bound to take a position on it; and a person who has read the analyses on this subject and heard the divergent points of view is bound to have a position on it. So it is with all the media: they are bound to leave their effect upon the one who hears them. This effect is partly positive and partly negative. The positive effect is when the media perform their true role in truthfulness of transmission in the news item, and are likewise objective in analysis, and likewise when there is no excess in following what one can do without. A person should restrict himself to what he cannot do without; if he goes beyond that to what he can do without, then the musical interludes and the advertisements for various kinds of trade and the like will swallow him up, and they too will take a space of his time and waste for him opportunities of his lifespan.

For this reason the discourse of the call must enter the media; and mere entry of this sort is not enough — that entry must be effective. For you know that the media today are no longer a means of cultivation only; rather, on the other side, they have also become a means of terror, and have become a means of war, and have also become a means of deception: the media are exploited for all of that. People have discovered, since the war on Islam in Afghanistan, the danger of the media; for the media are owned by the Westerners and are subject to them, and they have exploited them for war upon the Muslims and for deceiving them, so that they never convey the true news. I have mentioned to you an example of that before, along the lines of what the poet said: *"If they learn of good they hide it, and if they learn of evil they broadcast it; and if they learn nothing, they lie."* Or as the other said: *"If they hear an insult about me they fly with it in joy; and whatever they heard of good they buried. They are deaf when they hear a good thing I am mentioned for, and if I am mentioned to them with something bad, they have ears."*

So too with regard to deception: the media are now exploited to make things look good and to make things look ugly. Many of the fashions in clothing, in the cutting of hair and its styling, and even in the manner of speech and the way of pronunciation, are all broadcast by way of the media, and bands of people are influenced by them.

And likewise with regard to terror: on many occasions the media are a means of terror, whether that terror is intellectual — as you witnessed in the recent period in our media here, for their exploitation was a hideous exploitation for terror, intended to turn people away, to make them doubt their own opinions, and to make them doubt even their beliefs, and to make them doubt their convictions and many of the settled matters of their religion and their heritage, and to fabricate an imaginary war that has no basis at all and is supported by no evidence at all; and likewise to occupy people's whole time with what has no benefit in it, and to confine the debate — which it was important should be exact and scholarly — to questions that are settled matters and are not subjects of investigation, so that minds come round to supposing that they are subjects of investigation and of give and take, and it is asked what the opposing view on this question is, once interest in it has arisen. For it is familiar to people that the media have never on any day been attentive to jurisprudence, nor to legal theory, nor to hadith, nor to any of the other important scholarly disciplines; so when they see them concentrating on one discipline and summoning someone to debate that discipline, they suppose that there is something new in the matter, as if a new legislation had been sent down from the sky, or as if something unfamiliar to people had newly arisen in the matter.

Like that is the casting of doubt upon matters of religion. In our media in the recent campaign we heard someone say on television and on the radio that striving in the path of God (jihād) is void after the conquest of Mecca and is not lawful — and you certainly heard that; and this was repeated and broadcast again many times. This is plainly of the nature of intellectual terror, for it is a rejection of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and it is a claim that the expedition of Hunayn, the expedition of al-Ta'if, the expedition of Tabuk and the other expeditions in which the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) took part after the conquest of Mecca are all void and forbidden, and that the work of the Rightly Guided Caliphs likewise, in opening the easts and the wests of the earth, is all void. This would also entail the voidness of our own presence here: what brought us here to these lands — was it not striving in the path of God and campaigning to raise high the word of God? So the one who says this belies himself, because he sat here and spoke from this position only on account of striving in the path of God, which is what brought him to this place.

Like that too are some similar statements. We heard from among the speakers one who says that obedience to the one in authority is obligatory (wājib) so long as he does not command open unbelief; and this statement was put out to be heard on television and on the radio over and over again. This entails that if the one in authority commanded the drinking of wine, or fornication, or anything else, a person would be obliged to do it — because he said: obedience to him is obligatory so long as he does not command open unbelief. This may be an error of expression; its author may have intended something true and slipped into something false, of the plain falsehood in which there is no ambiguity, and no doubt its author does not believe it and would never want to say it. But the medium that repeated it and deliberately spread it and drew attention to it wanted it to be intellectual terror, overriding people's convictions and the fixed points of their religion and the matters that admit of no debate among them in any way whatsoever.

For this reason the discourse of the call must enter the media with strength, and with distinction too, so that they may be beneficial and effective; because if they are left with a free rein, what you have seen comes about. Either people boycott them and turn away from them — and then the loss occurs and a place in people's outlook and among their means remains unoccupied; or else they listen to them and take them with their lean and their fat, if there is any fat in them, and absorb them as they are — and this is an error and a great danger to their belief and to the settled matters of their religion. Hence there must be the selectiveness that can come about if a distinguished, moderate discourse of the call enters them.

The discourse of the call has varied and multiple media. You know that the internet, for example, is an open means for the discourse of the call, through which every person can offer his duty, and millions of people will see it without limits: it needs no visas and no travel tickets; rather the discourse reaches millions of human beings at the same moment, instead of people gathering for a lecture that they hear in a narrow place — each person hears it in his house and in the place where he is, without needing effort or travel. Like that are the tapes on which the discourse of the call is recorded: they have borne their fruit and proved their worth and spread through the easts and the wests of the earth, and have reached places one could not have imagined them reaching in any way at all. Indeed, praise be to God, they have become a pastime for many of the elderly who keep to themselves and are withdrawn: one of them takes a number of tapes and makes do with them in place of what used to happen formerly of his listening to old reports and past stories; so he listens to beneficial tapes, and perhaps finds in them what fills an emptiness for him and consoles him for his advanced age and the weakness of his body, or finds in them likewise what helps him to a good end and to adherence to the Sharia.

Likewise the fifth means influencing public opinion, which is companionship: there is no doubt that the discourse of the call must enter it with strength. This companionship is a duty imposed by reality upon human beings, for a person by his nature inclines towards his own human kind. It has come in the exegesis of Ibn Abbas concerning the saying of God Most High in Sūrat al-Naml: {I shall surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I shall slaughter him, or he shall bring me a clear authority} (Sūrat al-Naml 27:21) — what is this severe punishment? For the hoopoe is a weak bird; the punishment threatened cannot be an electric shock or a beating with sticks, for that would be killing it, and killing was mentioned in the slaughtering. So what is this punishing? He said: confinement with those not of his own kind. For a person's confinement with those not of his kind is a severe punishment in his case. Hence Muhammadhu ibn Muhammadi (may God Most High have mercy on him) says: *"Alas for a stranger in the west who has no kind of his own, even though he be surrounded by kinds."*

For this reason a person needs to mix with those who are at his level, and at that point he must be influenced and must influence. The task of the discourse of the call is that this being influenced and influencing should be positive. If a person influences others by his praiseworthy qualities, dealing with them well, addressing them with an address acceptable in the Sharia, sharing love and truthfulness with them, offering them the service he is able to offer and benefiting whomever he can benefit — this will undoubtedly have an influence, and his influence will be positive. And likewise his own being influenced by those he mixes with, if he is in this state: nothing seeps into him from the speech of the one he mixes with except what is praiseworthy and pleasing; so when he passes by idle talk he turns away from it, and when the ignorant address him he says "Peace". God has made that clear in His saying: {and those who do not bear false witness, and when they pass by idle talk they pass by with dignity} (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:72), and He said before it in these verses: {And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them they say "Peace"} (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:63).

So this person's being influenced must be a positive being influenced. But a person cannot do that unless he is fed with a strengthening that helps him to it, and this feeder ought to be an upright discourse of the call. You know that the society a person lives in — especially if it is like our mixed societies today — is one in which a person must encounter many viruses of faith and many specious arguments which he hears from others and picks up; and statements he hears which are mistaken and false but which are engraved on his outlook because he heard them from several quarters. So he needs a safety valve that repels the thorns and what has no benefit in it and separates them from his outlook entirely; and this valve must also be transparent, so that it does not prevent the truth from reaching him.

God has made this method clear in His saying: {So give good tidings to My servants — those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding} (Sūrat al-Zumar 39:17–18). {So give good tidings to My servants — those who listen to the word}: this requires a susceptibility to influence, in that the person listens to the word in the first place. Then after this, "and follow the best of it": they are not too proud to follow and to be influenced, because a statement is either correct or erroneous; if it is correct, then disdaining it is turning away from the truth, and if it is erroneous, then accepting it is likewise inclining to falsehood. Hence one must listen to the truth and then follow the best of it. {Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it. Those are the ones whom God has guided, and those are the people of understanding.} God has made clear two causes for that: the first cause is unseen and from God's own doing, namely guidance — {those are the ones whom God has guided}; and the second cause goes back to a person's own effort and action — {and those are the people of understanding}, meaning these are the ones who put their minds to work and so benefited from their experiences and were able to make their being influenced positive, since they put their minds to work and so took what benefited them and left what harmed them.

When a person puts his mind to work in this aspect, in selecting, then he will not be wholly withdrawn from people, wanting neither to influence nor to be influenced; and on the other hand, he will not be influenced except by what is correct and sound. In this correct manner of dealing with people, a person needs an effective discourse of the call that makes clear to him what mixing is appropriate, what being influenced is appropriate, and what statements he should listen to and what he should leave. For the human being is not like a beast led by its halter, nor is he like a predatory animal, like the wild beasts that cannot be led; rather the human being is a social creature capable of influencing and of being influenced. So in what concerns companionship and mixing, there must exist a discourse of the call that sets him right and is for him an encompassment that prevents him from deviating and a correction of his course in that.

Those who travel to distant countries and go out from their own environments and surroundings — such as students who study abroad, for example — in their first going out they witness the need for this kind of thing, because they had been in an environment in which they were accustomed to total dependency, and they came out of the neck of the bottle into total freedom all at once, and found themselves in an environment that had changed and in a pattern of life different from what they had been upon. They are in the greatest need of a new surrounding, which encircles them as the bracelet encircles the wrist, so as to guard them from evils, direct them to good, offer them successful experiences, and help them to get past obstacles and hindrances. Hence they never forget the merit of whoever does that for them at the outset, at the time of need for it.

Likewise, among the controls of this discourse of the call is that it must begin with the aspects that are agreed upon before the aspects that are disagreed upon. Whoever is being called, whoever he may be, must share with you many convictions and opinions; even if he is a Jew or a Christian, he shares some convictions with you. So begin first with what is agreed upon, and when that is firmly settled you have secured a ground for the discussion. In this discussion what is sought is persuasion, and that it be without terror, and that the one who takes it up takes it up with an argument that stays with him. God has made that clear in His Book in His saying: {And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the best way — except those of them who have done wrong — and say: We believe in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to you; our God and your God is one, and to Him we are submitted} (Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:46). The beginning here was with what is agreed upon: {say: We believe in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to you; our God and your God is one, and to Him we are submitted}. These are matters agreed upon between us and them, so we begin with them; and then afterwards we come to what is disagreed upon — {and to Him we are submitted}: this belongs to us specifically and not to them.

So too, with a Muslim who differs, one must begin after the points of agreement with the great settled matters, with the essential matters. The lesser matters in which people differ, most of which go back to independent reasoning, are in many cases subjects for independent reasoning (ijtihād), and investigation of them ought to be deferred; the discourse of the call ought not to make them a priority nor put them first. Rather, putting them first then entails division and differentiation, and does not benefit the call at all and offers it no advantage. Therefore, after the points of agreement, the concentration ought to be on the great matters.

You know that the conspiracies of unbelief against Islam today always try to occupy the Muslims with particulars and with what has no benefit in it, so that they defer the more important and begin with the lower. For example, in the negotiations between the Palestinians and the Jews in Palestine, the great points, which are the more important and which are a matter of life or death, include the question of the Aqsa Mosque: to whom does it belong? Is it for the Jews or for the Muslims? This question has not been discussed to this day; to this day it has not been put before any council for discussion nor for negotiation. The second question: those displaced from Palestine, who are six million dispersed throughout the world — will they return to their country or remain scattered for life? This question has not been discussed to this day. And so the great questions, which could ruin the cause and blow it up from its foundations, have not been reached by the discussion to this day, and all the agreements that have been signed to this day have not touched upon them. This kind of error, in beginning with the particulars and with the road map and with the powers of the Authority, and with what relates to funding and what relates to the security apparatus and cooperation, and so on — these are matters such that if agreement were reached on all their particulars and then a disagreement arose over one of the two preceding questions, the whole thing would be blown up. So why begin with them, and why concentrate on them, given their pettiness and their uselessness as regards agreement?

Comparable to this too are many of the particulars that people debate, especially the schools of da'wah with divergent framings — such as the question of democracy, for example. People pass over the great questions in it and begin with the particular questions and with the details, such as what relates to impugning persons and the standards of criticism, and they leave aside the great settled matters — for example, what relates to the foundations of change, and what relates to the foundations of government, and what relates to people's reality, and what relates to the desired alternative that ought to be put in place. These are great matters that people neglect in this field, so they begin with particulars that fall within the framework of these great universals; whereas if nothing remained of the points of disagreement but these particulars, no harm would have come about; and if agreement were reached on these particulars alone, the dispute would not be settled.

Therefore there must be liberation from illusions, and liberation likewise from living among the particulars in the whole affair, and a taking up of the great matters, their settled points and their foundations. If agreement is reached upon these foundations and great matters and upon what is settled by the evidence and by what is definitive, then there is no harm in disagreement over matters of independent reasoning, which are matters in which independent reasoning is admissible at that point; and it is possible to agree to defer them for a time, and then either the correct view becomes clear to one of the two parties, who returns to it, or they find means of settling the dispute between them.

Hence every scholarly discussion must be preceded by the preparing of a means of resolving disputes. Every group of people bound together by something in common must begin, as the first of its priorities, with what will settle disputes among them: what is the reference to which recourse is had when a dispute arises? For this reason the establishment of this reference comes in the Qur'an in a number of verses: {O you who believe, obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you; and if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you believe in God and the Last Day. That is better and fairer in outcome} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:59). And in His saying, Exalted is He: {And when there comes to them a matter of security or of fear, they broadcast it; whereas if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them, those among them who draw out conclusions would have known it} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:83). And in His saying: {The believers are only those who believe in God and His Messenger, and when they are with him upon a matter of collective concern do not depart until they have asked his leave. Those who ask your leave are the ones who believe in God and His Messenger. So when they ask your leave for some affair of theirs, give leave to whom you will among them and ask God's forgiveness for them; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful. Do not make the Messenger's calling you like your calling one another. God knows those of you who slip away under cover. So let those who go against his command beware lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment befall them} (Sūrat al-Nūr 24:62–63).

There must therefore be a concentration on the means of resolving a dispute when one arises — even in worldly matters. In matters of religion the means of resolving a dispute is recourse to the evidence, as we have explained, from the Book and the Sunnah. As for worldly matters that are subject to independent reasoning, and likewise particulars of religious matters that the texts have not settled, the reference in them must then have been settled beforehand. So if the reference is, for example, the view of the majority, then the preponderance is by the number of transmitters, as the scholars of hadith say, or the preponderance is by the overwhelming majority of those present. And even within these particulars it must also be made clear whether what is required is a simple majority, a relative majority or an absolute majority — all of these being majorities known in constitutional law, from what people have come to agree upon. All of that is among the things that prevent disputes arising and creeping in altogether.

So too in deciding an opinion in any respect whatsoever. The primitive means that existed among human beings in any of their views was that they issued from the command of their leader or their elder, and if they all opposed him he turned to their view, or if most of them opposed him he turned to their view. These may not be praiseworthy in their outcome, as Durayd ibn al-Simmah said: *"I gave them my command at the bend of the sand-dune, but they did not see the good counsel in it until the forenoon of the next day. And I am only of Ghaziyyah: if she goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghaziyyah goes right, I go right."*

Therefore the means of resolving disputes must be present in the mind, agreed upon and settled beforehand. In many of the discussions that take place, and especially with non-Muslims, I always stipulate before the discussion begins that our references be clear. I took the lesson from a report which al-Mubarrad transmits from Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) concerning his debate with the Kharijites, when he sat with them, Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) having sent him to them. Before entering into the statements of the Kharijites and debating them, he wanted to establish a clear ground, and so he said: "What do you hold against the cousin of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him)?" — meaning Ali ibn Abi Talib. They said: "Three things." He said: "You hold nothing else against him?" They said: "No." He said: "Do you see that if I were to show you by the evidence the soundness of what he is upon, you would return to him?" They said: "Yes." He said: "And whoever among you opposes that, what is upon him?" They said: "The curse of God and of the angels and of all mankind." So he said: "Then what are they?" They said: "The first is that he erased his own name from the caliphate." He said: "Do you not know that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) erased his own name from prophethood in the treaty of peace with Suhayl ibn Amr on the day of al-Hudaybiyah?" So they fell silent. He said: "That is one; and what is the second?" They said: "He defeated his enemy and did not divide the spoils." He said: "Do you see that, if the spoils had been divided, in whose share would the Mother of the Believers Aisha, for instance, have fallen?" So they put their hands over their faces out of shame at that. He said: "That is the second; and what is the third?" They said: "He made men arbitrators in the Book of God." He said: "Is the war of the community of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) and their fighting greater, or a hare killed in the sacred precinct?" They said: "Rather, a hare killed in the sacred precinct." He said: "Did God Most High not say in Sūrat al-Māʾidah: {two just men among you shall judge it, as an offering brought to the Kaaba, or an expiation of feeding the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting}?" (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:95). They said: "Yes indeed." So he established the argument against them and bound them by these three matters without the dispute being drawn out and without its splitting apart — bearing in mind that if he had entered into the particulars with them, they had been given a gift for disputation, and the matter would have been drawn out and would not have stopped at any limit.

Hence, so long as the outcomes are not made clear from the beginning and the general controls are not taken up before entering into the discussion, it will be an endless Byzantine wrangle, because it often leads also to departing from the point at issue, so that the discussion remains upon some other matter that has no connection with the subject, and there is a moving from one subject to another. This kind of thing is among the things the legal theorists (uṣūliyyūn) warn against: when the legal theorists laid down the rules of disputation, they made among the greatest of them what relates to arbitrary assertion, to overriding, and to departing from the question. For instance, the question at issue might be whether an intoxicant made from something other than grapes is forbidden (ḥarām) or not; and if this question is debated and the dispute branches out until it reaches the operative cause (ʿillah) of the prohibition of wine — whether it is intoxication or something other than intoxication — then this is a disagreement outside the point at issue, and does not lead to the very result required. And so on. Therefore, among the controls of the discourse of the call, it must be bound to a solid ground for discussion agreed upon between the two parties.

Likewise, among the controls of this discourse is that, on top of all that has preceded, the one who gives it must be stripped in it of all his emotions and his personal desires. For if a person acts, or presents his discourse, on the basis of his partisan zeal or his jealousy for his own side, he will always be bigoted for his group or his school, and this contradicts the proprieties of the general discourse of the call. A person must therefore strive that the discourse he presents be stripped of emotion. You may have what you love, and put your love where you wish; but even so, do not override the opinions of others and do not override their feelings, and know that the matter is wider than what has been mentioned.

Hence I recall that two men differed over one of the questions of the call, long ago, and one of the shaykhs was present and heard what they said; and when he saw the sharpness of each of them in his own opinion and his following of his own emotion, he said: "My two brothers, the Garden is vast — its breadth is the heavens and the earth — so it has room for the people of this opinion and for the people of the other opinion."

So when a person grasps that, and it becomes clear to him that mere overriding — saying "this is the correct view and this is what we take up and this is what so-and-so and so-and-so among people hold" — then the field has ceased to be an effective discourse of the call, and has become instead blind imitation and bigotry for a sect or for a party of people, and has become an overriding, as happens with many of the bigoted. You hear one of them, for instance, saying: "al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar is not of the people of the Sunnah." I have heard someone who, on being asked about al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, said: "He is not of the people of the Sunnah." So I asked him, saying: "What is the Sunnah, my brother?" He said: "The saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), his action and his tacit approval." I said: "If al-Hafiz is not of the people of the Prophet's saying, nor of his action, nor of his tacit approval, then you are certainly not of them."

Therefore a person must grasp here the danger of overriding, and the danger of not being stripped of emotion.

Likewise in this field a person must know how to distinguish between the fixed points of the Sharia and its variables. He must know that of the Sharia there is revelation sent down, protected from error; and of it there are the opinions of men, which admit of correctness and of error, and these opinions are not necessarily accepted in all their aspects but are subject to discussion, as Malik (may God have mercy on him) said: There is not one of us who does not refute and is not refuted, except the occupant of this grave.

And forgive us, for we have dealt with you as one slaughters a snake, by cutting off its head and its tail — being compelled to that; and perhaps there will be recompense, God willing, in the lessons to come.

flags.arabic: فليس التكفير مطلقا مذموما شرعا، بل التكفير المذموم شرعا هو تكفير المسلمين … أما تكفير الكافرين فهو غير مذموم شرعا، ولا يمكن أن يذمه عاقل
flags.context: In the passage on the unpraiseworthy reactions that immoderate preaching produces.
options: Translate in full and faithfully, as done here
Render only the first half of the distinction
flags.note: The Sheikh's point in context is a restriction: he is condemning people declaring one another unbelievers on no legal basis, and the second clause is his logical clarification that calling a non-Muslim a non-Muslim is a description, not an accusation. Read out of that context in English the sentence can be made to sound like a licence for takfīr, which is the opposite of what the passage argues. It has been rendered neither softened nor strengthened, and the surrounding context has been kept intact so that the restriction remains visible.

flags.arabic: إن الجهاد باطل بعد فتح مكة ولا يحل … وهذا من الإرهاب الفكري الواضح
flags.context: On what the Sheikh says was broadcast on local television and radio during 'the recent campaign'.
options: Translate in full and faithfully, as done here
flags.note: The Sheikh is refuting a claim made by others, not issuing a ruling on jihad. His argument is historical (the expeditions after the conquest of Mecca) and he draws no contemporary application whatsoever; none has been added. The passage nonetheless discusses jihad approvingly in a broadcast-media context and is the kind of text that carries risk when quoted in isolation in English.

flags.arabic: إن طاعة ولي الأمر واجبة ما لم يأمر بكفر بواح … وهذا مقتض لأن ولي الأمر إذا أمر بشرب الخمر أو بالزنا … وجب أن يفعله الإنسان
flags.context: On statements repeated in the broadcast media.
options: Translate faithfully, preserving that this is the Sheikh's criticism of the formulation
Render as though the Sheikh were stating the rule himself
flags.note: Attribution is critical here. The Sheikh is NOT saying that obedience to the ruler is owed unless he commands open unbelief; he is saying that this formulation, as broadcast, is an error whose consequence would be an obligation to obey a command to sin. He also says its author probably meant something true and would not hold what his words imply. Any English rendering that loses the reporting frame reverses his position on obedience to authority.

flags.arabic: المفاوضات بين الفلسطينيين واليهود في فلسطين … قضية المسجد الأقصى لمن يكون؟ … المهجرون من فلسطين وهم ستة ملايين
flags.context: An illustration of beginning with particulars instead of fundamentals.
options: Translate in full and faithfully, as done here
flags.note: Contemporary political content. It is used purely as an illustration of a methodological point about the order of negotiation. 'اليهود' has been rendered 'the Jews', which is what the Arabic says, rather than 'the Israelis'; the substitution would be a silent correction of the source. Dated to 2010; the figures and the state of negotiations are the Sheikh's, as of that date, and have not been updated.

flags.arabic: كما شهدتم في الفترة الماضية في وسائل إعلامنا هنا … الحملة الماضية
flags.context: The Sheikh's account of a media campaign in Mauritania.
options: Render as the Arabic has it, unidentified
flags.note: The Sheikh refers to a specific recent campaign in the Mauritanian media without naming it, any outlet, or any person. Nothing has been supplied to identify them. A reader in 2026 will not know what is referred to; a dated editorial note from the Sheikh's office, rather than from the translator, would be the right remedy.

flags.arabic: محمدُّ بن محمدي رحمه الله تعالى
flags.context: Attribution of the line of verse on the stranger who has no kin.
options: Muhammadhu ibn Muhammadi (transliterating the Mauritanian form محمدُّ)
flags.note: محمدُّ with the doubled final consonant is the characteristic Shinqiti form of the name, distinct from محمد. The transliteration preserves it. The poet is not further identified in the text; the Sheikh's office should confirm the form and the identification. Compare the similar unresolved Shinqiti attribution at ID 471.

flags.arabic: فلا وربك لا يؤمنون حتى يحكموك فيما شجر بينهم
flags.context: Introduced as a condition God placed upon faith.
options: Mark as a quotation in English and note the defect
Leave unmarked as the source leaves it
flags.note: Q 4:65, run into the prose without the ornate brackets used for every other Qur'anic quotation in this text. Same recurring source defect as at IDs 470 and 471. The marking in English is editorial; body_ar is unchanged.

translator_notes: Qur'anic renderings here are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.

al-khiṭāb al-daʿwī is rendered throughout as 'the discourse of the call', and daʿwah as 'calling people to Islam' on first occurrence. 'Discourse' is kept as a single fixed rendering because the whole lecture is a list of ḍawābiṭ (controls) upon it, and varying the term would break the structure.

The lecture is a transcript of a teaching session and ends with the Sheikh apologising for having compressed the material; he says he will make up what was left out in later lessons. Nothing has been added to fill that gap.
Lines of verse are rendered as prose in italics, per house style.
